Early blight typically appears on mature foliage rather than young leaves [3]. The disease usually infects the oldest (lower) leaves first, where symptoms begin as small, irregular to circular dark-brown spots [3]. The pathogen that causes late blight, Phytophthora infestans, infects a variety of Solanum spp., including eggplant, pepper, nightshades, and petunia. answer:
Yes, early blight on young potato leaves can be mistaken for late blight because lesions may reach up to 1/2 inch in diameter [2]. However, early blight lesions are angular and become restricted by leaf veins, whereas late blight lesions are circular and surrounded by collapsed pale or chlorotic tissue [4]. Additionally, early blight lesions often display dark concentric rings alternating with light-tan bands, a feature not characteristic of late blight [2].

answer:
The early blight fungus survives between growing seasons in infested plant debris, soil, and infected potato tubers [1]. It also persists in overwintering debris of susceptible solanaceous crops and weeds, including hairy nightshade [2]. The melanized spores and mycelia can withstand exposure to sunlight, drying, freezing, and thawing [3]. Infected seeds can also cause diseased plants, serving as a source for new spore production the following season [5]. If infected plants are not removed or incorporated into the soil at the end of the season, the fungus can survive in debris for at least one to several years [5].

In March 2007, it was identified for the first time in California and currently has a limited distribution. An educational brochure (PDF) was created at that time and is available to print. Infected tomato plants initially show stunted and erect or upright plant growth; plants infected at an early stage of growth will show severe stunting. However, the most diagnostic symptoms are those in leaves. Leaves of infected plants are small and curl upward; and show strong crumpling and interveinal and marginal yellowing . The internodes of infected plants become shortened and, together with the stunted growth, plants often take on a bushy appearance , which is sometimes referred to as 'bonsai' or broccoli'-like growth. Flowers formed on infected plants commonly do not develop and fall off (abscise). Fruit

Often the leaves on one portion of the plant (e.g., the top or the bottom) show severe symptoms, while those higher or lower in the plant are less affected. answer:
Holes or "shot holes" in tomato leaves can be caused by flea beetles, which create tiny round holes [1]. These insects are among the earliest emerging pests and jump away when disturbed [1]. Alternatively, holes may result from bacterial spot on fruit trees, where infected tissue dries out and tears away [2]. In both cases, symptoms include small spots that merge to make leaves appear scorched or ragged [1][2]. If you suspect a pest like flea beetles, use row cover fabric or insect mesh over plants from planting until flowering [1]. For bacterial spot, early defoliation is common on trees deficient in nitrogen or where the disease is complicated by pesticide injury [2]. Since no photo diagnosis is available, the specific cause remains uncertain [diagnosis]. You should check your plant's species and consult product labels for any treatments.

Target spot lesions develop dark concentric circles, often visually indistinguishable from early blight. Early blight, Septoria leaf spot, and target spot are caused by unrelated fungi. Infections are initiated when spores (conidia) land on susceptible tissues during warm, wet weather. Once tissues become infected, these fungi produce additional conidia, which continue to infect healthy tissues as long as pathogen-favorable conditions continue. answer:
Stems with sunken lesions may indicate early blight, where lesions are elliptical and can encircle stems causing distal tissue death [2]. They could also represent target spot, which causes small, watersoaked lesions that later become dark and crack, potentially leading to plant collapse [1]. Alternatively, the condition might be leaf scorch on strawberry, characterized by elongated, sunken, purplish-brown spots or streaks that can girdle petioles and kill leaves [3]. In soybeans, stem infections from frogeye leaf spot appear as long, narrow, dark lesions with flattened centers that turn gray to brown as they mature [5]. Tomato late blight can also cause firm, sunken lesions on stems, though these are often associated with mottled fruit and fuzzy pathogen growth [4]. Since no photo diagnosis is available, the specific condition remains uncertain [1]. For chemical control or disposal, always check the product label and local rules.

Byther Biology Several viruses can cause mosaic symptoms in tomatoes, including tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), tomato mosaic virus (ToMV), and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV). Symptoms caused by TMV and ToMV are similar. Leaves show green mottling and may be curled, stunted, and slightly deformed. Plants may be stunted and are generally somewhat yellowed. Fruit is not usually affected but may be small and ripen unevenly. An internal browning of fruit may also occur. TMV and ToMV can be spread by tools, hands, and clothing. Symptoms of CMV include leaves with yellow mottling, bushy and stunted plants, and a reduced yield of small, slow-to-mature fruit. answer:
A plant with a mosaic pattern on its leaves may have Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV), Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), or Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) [1][4]. Symptoms can include light or dark green mottling, leaf distortion, and stunting [1]. Leaves may also appear fern-like with raised dark green areas [1] or show yellow streaks and spots [2]. Fruit may ripen unevenly, develop brown spots, ringspots, or internal browning [2][4]. Management requires strict hygiene to prevent spread via tools, hands, clothing, or aphids (for CMV) [3][4]. Introduction Early blight occurs worldwide and is prevalent wherever potatoes are grown. Although the foliar phase of early blight was first reported in 1893, the tuber decay phase was not recognized until 1925. Foliar early blight and tuber decay are common in Colorado, Wyoming, and western Nebraska. Foliar early blight lesions decrease the leaf surface area, which reduces tuber yield potential. Although yield suppressions of 70 to 80 percent are reported, most losses rarely exceed 20 percent. Interaction of early blight with other diseases such as blackleg or Verticillium wilt can increase losses. Tuber infection and subsequent decay in storage can severely affect the quality of both fresh market and processing po- tatoes. Monitoring and control Effective management of early blight requires implementation of an integrated disease management approach. answer:
The "disease triangle" is the idea that a plant disease's incidence and severity depend on three factors: a susceptible plant variety (the host), a virulent disease-causing agent (the pathogen), and a favorable air and soil environment [1]. All three must occur simultaneously for disease to develop [1]. If any one side is missing, the disease fails to develop [2].

For example, planting a corn hybrid resistant to a given disease prevents that disease, because the susceptible-host side of the triangle is broken [2]. Common pathogen groups are fungi, bacteria, viruses, and nematodes [2]. Key environmental factors include air and soil temperature, rainfall, dew, relative humidity, soil type, soil pH, and soil fertility [2].

Crop Rotation Crop rotation is a sound cultural practice that also aids in the control of many diseases of corn (Nyvall, 1979). It is especially important for disease control when corn is grown in reduced tillage systems. A minimum of every other year in corn is neces- sary if crop rotation is to aid in disease control. Even then, rotation is not always effective because patho- gens (e.g., fungi causing leaf blights) can blow in from adjacent ﬁ elds. One popular cropping sequence where reduced tillage is practiced in the central and mid-southern U.S. is the production of three crops in 2 years (e.g., corn the ﬁ rst year then small grains and soybean double- cropped the second year). answer:
Crop rotation helps because corn residue is a source of inoculum for disease, and rotation plus good residue management can reduce in-field sources of it [2]. Pathogens can overwinter in crop residue and infect corn the following growing season [3]. Rotating away from corn breaks that cycle.

Rotation is especially important when corn is grown in reduced tillage systems [1]. In no-till or reduced-till fields with a history of northern corn leaf blight, a two-year rotation out of corn may be needed to reduce disease in the next corn crop [4]. For gray leaf spot, a two-year rotation away from corn is effective if reduced tillage must be maintained [5].

Rotation is not always fully effective, because fungi that cause leaf blights can blow in from adjacent fields [1]. Some cropping sequences are not true rotations for certain pathogens: the Gibberella ear and stalk rot fungus also infects small grains, and the charcoal stalk rot fungus also infects soybean [3].

Generally, infected plants have a light or dark green mottling or mosaic with distortion of younger leaves, and stunting to varying degrees. Severely affected leaves may have a “fern- like” appearance and may show raised dark green areas. Fruit set may be severely reduced in affected plants.
